Overview

Amyloid

Misfolded protein that deposits in extracellular space

Damages tissues

Amyloidosis

Multiple proteins can deposit as amyloid

β- pleated sheet configuration

Congo red staining and apple-green birefringence under polarized light

Classification

Primary amyloidosis

Systemic deposition of AL amyloid, derived from Ig light chain

Associated with plasma cell proliferations

Organs affected include heart, GI tract, respiratory tract, peripheral nerves, skin and tongue

Reactive Systemic Amyloidosis (secondary)

Systemic deposition of AA amyloid derived from SAA

SAA is an acute phase reactant that is increased in chronic inflammatory states, malignancy

Organs affected include kidneys, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, adrenal glands and thyroid glands

Heredofamilial Amyloidosis

Variety of familial forms of amyloidosis are described but most are rare, the most common being familial Mediterranean fever (FMF)

FMF is autosomal recessive, autoinflammatory syndrome, characterized by excessive production of cytokine IL-1

Familial Mediterranean Fever

Presents with episodes of fever and acute serosal inflammation

High SAA during attacks deposits as AA amyloid

Organs affected include kidneys, blood vessels, spleen, respiratory tract, and (rarely) liver.

Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (Familial amyloid cardiomyopathy)

Mutated serum transthyretin deposits in heart

Leads to restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias

4% of African Americans carry mutated gene and penetrance differs substantially among individuals; some have severe disease while others have no disease at all

Senile systemic amyloidosis (Senile cardiac amyloidosis)

Non mutated serum transthyretin (TTR) deposits occur with aging

Usually asymptomatic but if symptomatic it present with restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias

Clinical findings

Renal involvement: most affected organ, proteinuria

Cardiac involvement: Restrictive cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia

GI involvement: Tongue enlargement, malabsorption, and hepatosplenomegaly

Vascular involvement: vessels fragility

Diagnosis

Dx is based on histopathology: H&E stain shows amyloid as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline extracellular substance, while it appears red in color under ordinary light using Congo red stain and apple green birefringence under polarized light using the same stain

Commonly biopsied sites include the kidneys, rectum, gingival tissue, abdominal fat pads

Serum and urine protein electrophoresis

Bone marrow examination

Scintigraphy with radiolabeled SAP

Mass spectrometry

Treatment

Damaged organs must be transplanted

Amyloid cannot be removed

Prognosis

Prognosis of generalized amyloidosis is poor

AL amyloidosis without MM median survival is 2 years after diagnosis while those with MM have worse prognosis

Reactive systemic amyloidosis has a better prognosis generally

Localized and other forms

Localized amyloidosis

Amyloid deposition usually localized to a single organ

Lung, larynx, skin, urinary bladder, tongue and region around the eye maybe affected

Frequently, infiltrates of lymphocytes and plasma cells a/w these amyloid masses

In some cases, the amyloid consist of AL amyloid, and therefore represent a localized form of plasma cell derived amyloid

Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus

Amylin deposits in islets of pancreas

Derived from insulin

Medullary carcinoma of thyroid

Calcitonin deposits within tumor

Alzheimer disease

Aβ amyloid deposits in brain, forming amyloid plaques

Derived from β- amyloid precursor protein (on chromosome 21)

Dialysis-associated amyloidosis

β2- macroglobulin deposits in joints
